text: Every storage account picks a redundancy option, and the tradeoff behind every one of them is the same: cost versus durability. Locally Redundant Storage, LRS, keeps three synchronous copies of your data within a single datacenter in your chosen region. It's the cheapest option on the table, and it protects you against ordinary drive and rack-level hardware failure — but it does not protect you if that one datacenter itself goes down.

Zone-Redundant Storage, ZRS, also keeps three copies, but spreads them synchronously across separate Availability Zones within that same region — the same Availability Zones you met back in Chapter 3 protecting VM resilience. That means a single datacenter failure no longer threatens your data at all, because the data was never only sitting in one physical building to begin with, for a fairly modest cost increase over plain LRS.

Geo-Redundant Storage, GRS, takes an LRS copy in your primary region and asynchronously replicates a second LRS copy to Azure's designated paired region, often hundreds of miles away. That's real protection against a regional disaster, the kind of event ZRS genuinely cannot survive since it never leaves the region. The real tradeoff is cost, because you're now paying for storage footprints in two separate regions, plus the fact that replication is asynchronous, so the very newest writes could theoretically be lost in a true regional failure.

Change a storage account's redundancy option at any time with az storage account update and a new SKU such as Standard_GRS. Once durability is covered, the other half of this lesson automates something manual from Lesson 14: instead of moving backup blobs from Hot to Cool to Archive by hand on a schedule you keep track of yourself, a lifecycle management policy does it for you.

One policy, created with az storage account management-policy create, encodes that entire plan in a single rule: tier to Cool after seven days, tier to Archive after ninety days, delete the blob outright after a year. Azure evaluates that rule continuously against every matching blob, with no human ever touching a blob's tier by hand again.

LRS, ZRS, GRS, and lifecycle management policies close out everything this chapter set out to cover in Azure Storage. Next chapter turns to networking: virtual networks and subnets, building the real network that the virtual machines and storage accounts from these last two chapters actually live inside.
